title: tem, tenho, entende
explanation: These three words all show ten or tem on the page, but the letters are doing different jobs. In Brazilian Portuguese as spoken in Rio and São Paulo: tem ends in a nasal diphthong, not a consonant m; in tenho the n belongs to nh (a palatal “ny”) and the vowel before it is nasal; in entende each en is a nasal vowel with no n consonant, and final de is pronounced “jee.”

title: é and e
explanation: The accent is the whole difference, in both spelling and sound. é (with an accent) is the verb “is,” an open eh [ɛ]. e (no accent) is the conjunction “and,” and sounds like ee [i]. Mixing them up changes the word.

title: sei and sabe
explanation: Two present-tense forms of saber, with different vowel letters and different sounds. sei is a diphthong [sej], like English “say.” sabe is SAH-bee [ˈsabi]: the final unstressed e is pronounced [i], and the b stays a plain b.

title: muito’s hidden nasal
explanation: muito has no tilde, but the ui is still a nasal diphthong [ũj]. Brazilians say something like MOOYN-too [ˈmũjtu], not “moo-ee-too.” This is a well-known quirk of the spelling.

title: não and no
explanation: não “no / not” has a tilde: the ão is a nasal diphthong [ɐ̃w̃], like a nasal “own.” no is a different word, the contraction em + o (“in the”), and is just [nu], like “new” without the glide. The tilde is not decoration.

title: o and ó
explanation: The letter o does not have one sound. The article o (“the”) is unstressed and pronounced [u], like “oo.” The accented ó, as in dólar, is an open o [ɔ], like the vowel in English “thought” (or a rounder “aw”). Same letter, two sounds; the accent on ó marks the open one.

title: Numbers: 11–19, 20, 100
explanation: From 11 to 15, Portuguese uses irregular -ze forms inherited from Latin -decim (‘ten’): onze, doze, treze, catorze, quinze. At 16 the pattern becomes transparent: dezesseis is dez e seis, and the same ‘ten and…’ run goes through dezenove. vinte is a new word (Latin vīgintī), not *dez e dez. cem is the stand-alone 100; before another number the form is cento (cento e um). Pronunciation is Rio / São Paulo.

title: isso and isto
explanation: These two look like a single letter’s difference, and they are. isto keeps a t: [ˈistu], ‘this’ near the speaker. isso has no t: [ˈisu], ‘that’ near the listener. In casual Brazilian speech isso often covers both meanings, but the t is still the whole difference in how they are said. (aquilo, ‘that over there,’ is the third of the set.)

title: que and quem
explanation: que (‘what’) is a short [ki], like “kee” — no nasal. quem (‘who’) looks like que plus m, but that -em is not a consonant m. It is the same nasal diphthong as in tem: [kẽj̃]. Mixing them up changes the question (what vs who).
